newsitem.title: LEBANON: FOCUS - Credit ratings divide Beirut market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Credit ratings divide Beirut market.

text.p: International credit agencies gave Lebanon its first credit ratings on Wednesday and Beirut bankers were divided over whether the country got a fair deal.
Moody's, Standard & Poor's, the European agency IBCA and Japan's NIS gave Lebanon's longterm foreign currency debt high "speculative grade" ratings.
The government appeared satisfied, saying in a statement that the ratings put Lebanon on a par with countries like Argentina and Jordan and ahead of Turkey, Brazil, Peru, Bulgaria and Pakistan.
At Lebanon Invest finance house, Corporate Finance Manager Bassam Yammine called it a fair assessment for a country returning to the international capital markets after a long absence.
"I'm not disappointed. I'm not excited. I think it's fine as a start," Yammine told Reuters.

"I believe the ratings are as expected.....Everybody would have hoped for Triple B (investment grade) or up, but Lebanon is not ready to be there because it has been absent from the capital markets for years and it's only just coming back, he said."
Freddie Baz, a director of Banque Audi, a leading Beirut bank, said he was not surprised by the ratings but he was a little disappointed.
"I think it's not fair, we deserve at least one notch more if not two notches more," he said.

"I would never have expected investment grade rating but I consider BB+ or BB with a positive outlook would have been a fair rating for Lebanon," he said. "Lebanon deserves to get the upper limit of the speculative grade."

Baz said the credit agencies had failed to understand the Lebanese economy fully and there were additional elements they should have considered in their assessments. "You can't assess Lebanon the same way as other countries," he said.

The ratings were the first granted to Lebanon, whose government and banks have successfully tapped the international capital markets in the past two years to help finance its recovery from the devastating 1975-90 civil war.

The government has raised $800 million in Eurobonds since 1995 and commercial banks have raised close to $500 million in Eurobonds and EuroCds in the past year despite the fact that the country had no credit rating. Several banks have also made successful international share issues.
A government spokesman said the ratings were an important part of Lebanon's rehabilitation and of its effort to mobilise increased financial resources for reconstruction and investment.
Standard and Poor's gave a BB minus rating, citing heavy budget deficits, soaring public debt and a vulnerable fiscal system as constraints.
It said things could get better although the geopolitical situation still posed risks to national reconstruction.

Moody's gave a B1 rating, citing Lebanon's fragile public sector finances and the massive reconstruction effort needed after the civil war. The European agency IBCA awarded a BB and Japan's NIS a BBB-.
"The thing is these are the first ratings," Yammine said. "I believe periodic revisions in the future will upgrade Lebanon because the country is definitely on the right track."
Ziad Makkawi, managing director and head of capital markets at Middle East Capital Group, a Beirut finance house, doubted that the ratings would have much impact on the price of Lebanese debt.
"My feeling is that people have been buying Lebanese paper without ratings amd the appetite for Lebanese paper will continue," he said.
"If there is a price reaction it might be very short. The spreads on Lebanese bonds have already tightened incredibly and it's not clear if this will affect the price of future issues," Makkawi said.
